source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models (ICLR) - where the lost tasks go
finding: A correct hypothesis was in the pool for about half of ARC tasks, but fewer became correct programs. The loss has two parts: picking the hypothesis, and turning it into code.
numbers: 100 ARC tasks, GPT-4, 64 hypotheses per task. Human annotators found a correct hypothesis in 49 tasks. With a human choosing the hypothesis, 33 of 49 (67%) became correct programs after up to 3 rounds of execution feedback (accuracy by feedback round 26, 31, 33, 33). With GPT-4 summarising 64 hypotheses into 8, 30 tasks were solved; 28 of those had a correct hypothesis before summarising. Direct prompting 17%, programs only 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected 33%, human-written 33%.
limits: One model (GPT-4), 100 tasks, human annotators judge hypothesis correctness. Of the 16 lost after human selection, the paper points at program generation (hard tasks, spatial symmetry), not hypothesis choice. Summarising sometimes dropped the correct hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Most of the gap between 'right idea in the pool' and 'right program' is implementation, not selection. An LLM-side selector loses only about 3 tasks (30 vs 33); the other 16 need a better implementer, more feedback, or a different representation.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search, appendix B.4: LLM likelihood reranking of hypotheses
finding: A model-based reranker did a poor job of finding the correct hypothesis in the pool. Scoring each hypothesis by how likely it makes the examples did not let the authors throw away bad hypotheses.
numbers: GPT-3 reranked GPT-4 hypotheses by probability of generating the input-output examples given the hypothesis. On the 21 tasks where one of 64 candidates was correct, the correct hypothesis was in the top 16 for only 10 tasks. The share of tasks with a correct hypothesis rises steadily with more samples but the slope flattens (Fig A.6).
limits: Pilot, 21 tasks, one reranker design, reported by the authors as a non-systematic finding.
agent_relevance: Blind model scoring of a pool is weak: about half the right hypotheses fall outside the top quarter. Execution against the examples (G3) is a sharper tool than a likelihood judge.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample right) keeps rising with more samples, but selection by majority vote or a reward model stalls. Without an automatic verifier the gap between 'in the pool' and 'chosen' grows with pool size.
numbers: MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward-model selection only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range; plateau near 100 samples. Gemma-2B on CodeContests: coverage up over 300x from 0.02% at one sample. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples) vs single-sample state of the art 43%, where unit tests act as the verifier.
quote: two common methods for verification (majority voting and reward models) do not possess this ability
limits: The reward model was ArmoRM-Llama3-8B. Models are 2024-era open models. Where a real verifier exists coverage turns into accuracy.
agent_relevance: This is the cleanest measurement of the recoverable gap. A code-run check that tells right from wrong is worth more than any vote or judge, and without one extra samples are wasted.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, section 4: verifier imperfections
finding: Test-based checks are not perfect. Flaky or too narrow tests give false positives and false negatives that cap what code gating can recover.
numbers: 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems have flaky test suites that sometimes mark even the gold fix wrong. CodeContests has false negatives because tests demand one output when many are valid. Majority vote picks the right answer on problems where right samples are common and misses those where right samples are rare (Fig 8).
limits: Descriptive audit by the authors, not a controlled experiment.
agent_relevance: A G3 gate must be audited for its own error rate. A weak or narrow check rejects correct explanations and passes lucky wrong ones.

source: Li, Hu, Larsen, Wu, Alford, Woo, Dunn, Tang, Naim, Nguyen, Zheng, Tavares, Pu, Ellis (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Induction (write a function that explains the examples, then run it) and transduction (predict the test output directly) solve different ARC problems. A cheap gate joins them: use induction if some candidate function fits the training examples, else fall back to transduction.
numbers: Same architecture and data. Table 1 (validation, 2 tries): induction 18.78%, transduction 15.25%, ensemble 26.50% (GPT-4 descriptions); second data setting induction 11.07%, transduction 13.50%, ensemble 19.50%. About 9% of samples that fit the training examples are false positives; about half of those still lose to a majority vote over outputs. Scaled models reach 56.75% ensemble vs average human 60.2% (best human 97.8%). Induction gains almost monotonically with more samples.
quote: Induction first, then transduction if none of the candidate hypotheses explained the examples
limits: Trained neural models on synthetic ARC variants, not prompted frontier models. Table 2 is garbled in the PDF text, so only Table 1 and the text figures are used.
agent_relevance: 'Does any hypothesis fit the examples' is a free, code-run switch between hypothesis mode and direct mode. It also checks whether the pool holds a candidate at all.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction, section 6: which problems suit which mode
finding: Hypothesis-then-test wins on precise computation and on composing several concepts. Direct prediction wins on fuzzy perceptual concepts and on single-concept tasks.
numbers: ConceptARC (one concept per problem): counting and similar symbolic concepts are best solved by code; judging whether a shape is more horizontal or vertical, or top versus bottom, is better with transduction. Induction loses its edge on ConceptARC because there is no need to compose concepts. Authors: neither mode covers all cases and a simple ensemble does not close the gap.
limits: Per-concept charts only (Fig 10); no single predictor score is given. Trained models, not prompted ones.
agent_relevance: A usable S0 rule: send problems with precise, countable, composable structure to hypothesis-then-test; send perceptual, single-pattern problems to direct answering or to a different explanation language.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Hu, Ren, Lu, Choi, Sap, Kim, Choi (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR) - signs by task
finding: Iterative hypothesis refinement with a code interpreter helps on rule tasks and hurts on MiniARC raw accuracy. On MiniARC the model's rules are verbose and hard to read, while humans use pragmatic concepts such as 'drop', 'mirror', 'Tetris'.
numbers: GPT-4. Raw accuracy, IO prompting vs refinement (T=3 rounds, N=5 hypotheses): ACRE 64.0 vs 82.5; List Functions 65.1 vs 71.2; MiniARC 33.1 vs 18.7. Task accuracy: ACRE 28.0 vs 59.0; List Functions 39.6 vs 61.2; MiniARC 13.8 vs 14.6. MiniARC with T=1,N=1 is 5.9 raw. Self-refine with an LM as interpreter: MiniARC 15.1 raw. Natural-language vs Python hypotheses are about equal (MiniARC 18.7 vs 18.1). Weaker models (GPT-3.5, Claude-2, LLaMA2-70B) lag on complex rules.
limits: Authors suggest MiniARC rewards pattern matching and needs visual understanding; text-only models see grids as text. Task-specific heuristics made rules more readable but the gain was limited.
agent_relevance: The sign of the effect follows how well the true rule can be stated. Where a short symbolic rule exists, test it. Where the structure is visual or pattern-like and the model cannot name it, refinement can lose to plain prompting.

source: Hua, Wong, Sun, Pan, Jardine, Wang (2025) InductionBench: LLMs Fail in the Simplest Complexity Class
finding: Even reasoning models fail to recover the simplest function classes in the subregular hierarchy once the rule needs a slightly wider context window. Difficulty rises with the number of rules and with the window size k.
numbers: Setting k=4, vocabulary 4, 3 rules, sample twice the minimal characteristic sample: compatibility collapses to 0 for every model except o3-mini. Leaderboard compatibility for o3-mini 5.69% overall, because no model succeeds when k=4. o1-mini and o3-mini show non-trivial recall and precision but compatibility near zero on harder settings.
limits: String-to-string functions, synthetic. Models tested: o1-mini, o3-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Llama 3.x.
agent_relevance: Rule complexity (description length, number of rules) is a measurable predictor of failure of hypothesis search. S0 could estimate the rules or window width a task seems to need and fall back to a safer mode when it is high.

source: Wei, Suresh, Cao, Kannan, Wu, Yan, Teixeira, Wang, Aiken (2025) CodeARC: Benchmarking Reasoning Capabilities of LLM Agents for Inductive Program Synthesis (COLM)
finding: Passing the given examples is a weak gate. Many programs fit all shown examples and still differ from the target. A differential-testing oracle that returns new counterexamples is a much stricter held-out check.
numbers: 1114 functions, 18 models; best o3-mini 52.7% on the anonymised set (59.5% on the annotated set). For o3-mini's first synthesised function: 1506 problems (67.6%) pass the 10 initial examples but only 866 (38.9%) pass the oracle, so 640 (28.7%) are underspecified by the examples. One row of Table 4 shows o3-mini at 51.3, 53.8, 56.1 with 10, 20, 30 observable examples (row alignment uncertain).
limits: The oracle is two differential-testing tools, which cannot be perfect (program equivalence is undecidable). Table 4 columns are garbled in the text.
agent_relevance: Supports the held-out gate (G3): fit on the seen examples is not enough, the gate must test on fresh cases. It also sizes the false-accept problem at about 29 points for the best model.

source: Chen, Aksitov, Alon, Ren, Xiao, Yin, Prakash, Sutton, Wang, Zhou (2023) Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
finding: Asking the model to judge which of its own candidates is most consistent matches ordinary vote counting where a vote is possible, and leaves a large gap to the oracle choice.
numbers: Eight samples, PaLM 2-L. GSM8K: greedy 85.7, SC 90.4, USC 90.2, oracle 96.2. MATH: greedy 30.8, SC 37.9, USC 37.4, oracle 57.2. BIRD-SQL (gpt-3.5-turbo) execution accuracy: greedy 42.4, SC-Exec 45.6, USC 45.5, oracle 53.3. Random pick from the pool is below greedy (GSM8K 82.9).
limits: Old models and answers that have a clear format. It does not test virtue-based scores.
agent_relevance: A blind model judge is about as good as voting and about as far from the oracle. The real target for a code-computed score is the oracle gap (about 6 points on GSM8K, about 20 on MATH).

source: Chen et al. (2022) CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests (ICLR 2023)
finding: A selection score computed by running code, from dual agreement (a solution passes many model-written tests and agrees with many other solutions), beats earlier selection methods.
numbers: code-davinci-002, pass@1 on HumanEval 47.0% to 65.8% (+18.8 absolute), MBPP 58.1% to 67.7%. Codex pass@100 was 77.4% on HumanEval while pass@1 was much lower, which is the pool-versus-pick gap.
limits: Code tasks with executable semantics; the tests are written by the same model and can be wrong.
agent_relevance: Set-level agreement is a code-computed, inference-time selection rule. It is the nearest direct example of the S7 idea in gap 8: score a candidate by how well it agrees with the other candidates and the tests, not by a single judge.

source: Nitarach (2026) Model Capability Dominates: Inference-Time Optimization Lessons from AIMO 3
finding: Prompt diversity among voters did not help. The gap between the best majority-vote score and pass@20 is selection loss that needs a verifier, not better prompts.
numbers: 50 IMO-level problems, 3 models, 23+ experiments. gpt-oss-120b N=8: per-attempt accuracy 0.69, score 39.3 (21 runs); best majority-vote 42/50 vs pass@20 45.5. gpt-oss-20b 31.0 at N=8, down to 26 at N=32. Code-first prompt got 41, 38, 34 across three runs (mean 37.7, below baseline).
limits: Preprint by one author, small problem set, competition-style math.
agent_relevance: On hard problems the cap is the model, and selection among samples is the next bottleneck. Prompt tricks to diversify explanations did not fix it.

source: Li and Li (2026) From Discovery to Decision: Finite-Budget Recoverability in LLM Voting
finding: Often the correct answer is found in the sample but never wins the vote. Exact, code-checkable filters on the pool can recover answers without hurting any.
numbers: Between 2% and 46% of trajectories that sample the correct answer end with a wrong plurality output (by task). MATH: 70B coverage rises 80.0% to 95.2% from B=16 to 1,024 while plurality accuracy stays near 60%. Word16 (4B model, 256 paired items): input permutation raises plurality accuracy 57.42% to 78.52% (+21.09 points, bootstrap 95% CI 14.06 to 28.12). An exact multiset check on a Word16 pool raises plurality accuracy 74.2% to 92.2%, correcting 69 inputs and damaging none.
limits: Word16 is a controlled toy task where an exact check exists. Late discoveries still convert: GSM converts 41 of 219 (18.7%).
agent_relevance: When a strict code check exists, filtering before voting recovers most of the lost share; when it does not, expect a large unrecovered loss.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse (ICML 2025)
finding: A human result (explaining pushes learners to broad rules and hurts when the data have exceptions; Williams, Lombrozo and Rehder 2013) carries over to LLM chain of thought. CoT models keep applying the broad rule and need more passes to learn the exceptions.
numbers: Vehicle classification, 80% rule and exceptions, 2400 vehicles in 240 lists. Mean rounds to learn all labels, direct vs CoT: GPT-4o 2.9 vs 12.5 (+331%, p<0.0001), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4 (+178%), Claude 3 Opus 2.4 vs 5.5 (+129%). GPT-4o with CoT stagnated at 80% correct per round. Same paper: o1-preview loses 36.3 points on implicit pattern learning (artificial grammar) vs GPT-4o; on face recognition CoT cut GPT-4o from 64.00% to 51.20%.
quote: CoT stagnates at 80%, the proportion which are not exceptions.
limits: 2024 models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, o1-preview on subsets). CoT effects were mixed or neutral on other tasks. Authors say the heuristic does not predict every case.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 9: asking a model to explain before it predicts can lock it onto one unifying rule and leave exceptions unlearned. S2 should keep a separate store of cases that break the rule.

source: Kirichenko, Ibrahim, Chaudhuri, Bell (2025) AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
finding: Models rarely say 'no answer fits' and reasoning training makes it worse. This is the bad-lot problem in general form, tested on 20 datasets and more than 35,000 unanswerable questions.
numbers: 20 frontier models. Reasoning fine-tuning lowers abstention recall by 24% on average (DeepSeek-R1 Distill Llama 70B and s1 vs non-reasoning counterparts). Scaling the reasoning token budget raises accuracy but generally further worsens abstention. Recall ranges from near perfect (BIG-Bench Known Unknowns) to near zero (MediQ). A carefully written system prompt raises abstention but does not fix the underlying problem. Models often hallucinate missing context.
limits: The task is unanswerable questions, not candidate pools with no true explanation. Scoring uses an LLM judge (Llama 3.1 8B).
agent_relevance: The model's own sense that nothing fits is not reliable. A bad-lot gate should come from code (no candidate fits the data), not from model confidence.

source: Hashemi, Bamgbose, Madhusudhan, Nair, Tiwari, Yadav (2025) DNR Bench: Benchmarking Over-Reasoning in Reasoning LLMs
finding: Reasoning models fail to say 'unanswerable' when asked plainly, but a short instruction to flag flawed questions recovers a lot for some of them. Reasoning models also spend far more tokens.
numbers: 150 adversarial prompts; the Unanswerable category has 50 items. Accuracy without / with instruction: GPT-4o 0.42 / 0.98; Claude-3.7-Thinking 0.12 / 0.82; DeepSeek-R1 0.00 / 0.20; o3-mini-high 0.00 / 0.02; R1-Distill-Llama-70B 0.06 / 0.62. Abstract: reasoning models use up to 70x more tokens than needed.
limits: Short, easy-for-humans prompts; correct means the model explicitly says the problem is unanswerable. Not about explanation pools.
agent_relevance: A no-explanation outcome has to be a named legal answer in the prompt, and even then some reasoning models ignore it. Treat 'none fits' as an output state that code can set.

source: Cooper, Sadhu, Velasquez (2026) DeFAb: A Dataset for Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
finding: A code-checked test of 'the edit resolves the conflict and keeps other predictions' can be passed by a trivial entity-specific exception. Passing the check does not show the model chose a good scope.
numbers: Held-out panel of 336 tasks (150 L1, 150 L2, 36 L3); simple symbolic repairs solve all 336. Two of six model deployments succeed on every task under both prompt styles. Prompt style matters a lot: one row (Claude Sonnet 5.5) shows 133 of 336 direct vs 336 of 336 structured. All 3,144,222 rule bodies in the release are a single entity fact, which permits the entity-local shortcut.
limits: A preprint; its planned studies are not yet run, and the authors call the released test flawed. Table text is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Warning for gap 9 and G3: a verifier that only checks the observed case rewards local fixes (this penguin) over the right scope (penguins). A held-out transfer set is needed, with cases that must change and cases that must stay.

source: Reddy, Challaram, Basu (2026) Reason Less, Verify More: Deterministic Gates Recover a Silent Policy-Violation Failure Mode in Tool-Using LLM Agents
finding: Deterministic read-only gates that check an action before it runs raise success, but the lift comes from one high-precision gate. A second gate had 5% precision, so every gate must be audited.
numbers: tau-bench airline domain. gpt-4o-mini success 29.6% to 42.0% with four gates (+12.4 points, 95% CI 4.0 to 21.2); replicated on disjoint seeds, +12.3. One gate had 100% precision over 161 fires; another 5%. Gates fire on 26 of 50 tasks, +19.2 points there; non-firing tasks not clearly changed. Frontier agent 61.2% to 71.6% (n=5, no replication). Gates help where tools accept any call, add little in a self-enforcing retail domain and BFCL.
limits: Tool-use agents, not explanation selection. Gates were tuned on one model.
agent_relevance: Supports code gates at S7/G3 with a precision audit: measure how often each gate fires and how often it is right before trusting it.

source: Trpin and Pellert (2019) Inference to the Best Explanation in Uncertain Evidential Situations (BJPS) - full text read
finding: Confirms the early-overconfidence problem and shows that only one bonus size was tried. The explanationist agent reacts boldly at the start and is often led astray before it recovers.
numbers: Table 7: share of runs where the agent first assigned probability above 0.95 to a false hypothesis: IBE** 233,882 (47%) vs JC (Jeffrey) 15,401 (3%); above 0.99: IBE** 184,437 (37%) vs JC 5,779 (1%). Table 1 (55,000 runs; column labels garbled, mapping inferred from the row totals): Pr(true)>0.95 JC 16%, IBE** 52%; >0.99 JC 11%, IBE** 49%; Pr(false)>0.95 JC 24%, IBE** 30%; >0.99 JC 17%, IBE** 22%. Brier score: IBE** converges toward 0, JC stays near 1.06.
quote: is thus often initially lead astray
limits: Footnote 11: bonus fixed at 0.1 following Douven; 'a systematic investigation is beyond the scope'. The authors say the bonus size is future work. Coin-bias simulations only.
agent_relevance: The bonus size was never varied here, so gap 5 is not answered by this paper. Practical lesson: bold early commitment is often wrong, so S7 should not commit on a bonus alone before held-out evidence.

source: Douven (2020) The ecological rationality of explanatory reasoning (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science)
finding: The best explanatory bonus depends on the setting. In an evolutionary simulation of ICU diagnosis it came out about ten times smaller than the 0.1 default. Agents with a large bonus died out early; those that survived the early phase then did best.
numbers: Initial bonuses c drawn from U(0, 0.25). Last-generation EMMs: EXPL users c = 0.010 (95% CI 0.010 to 0.011), Good's rule 0.117, Popper's rule 0.227. Fitness EMM EXPL 0.873 vs Good 0.871, Popper 0.872 (differences p<0.0001, eta-squared .002). Equivalent to 24 extra lives per 10,000 patients vs Good's rule and 14 vs Popper's. EXPL users drop sharply in number shortly after the start before recovering. Setting c = 0 gives Bayes' rule.
limits: Simulated ICU doctors, not LLMs; small fitness differences; the optimum is specific to the setting. Douven treats the bonus as a context-tuned parameter.
agent_relevance: Answer to gap 5 in outline: keep any explanatory bonus small (order 0.01, not 0.1), tune it per setting, expect early-phase errors. For S7 a bonus that only breaks ties between rules with similar support.

source: Lim and Oppenheimer (2020) Explanatory preferences for complexity matching (PLoS ONE) - independent lab
finding: Outside the Lombrozo lab, people did not simply prefer simple explanations. They preferred explanations about as complex as the event. This reconciles Lombrozo (simple preferred) with Zemla et al. (complex preferred).
numbers: Four studies on Mechanical Turk. Study 1 n=286 (predicted complexity of a satisfying explanation; complex scenarios rated more complex, M 5.67 vs 4.88, chi2(1)=38.02). Study 2 n=201 (written explanations). Study 3 n=523 (satisfaction: each unit of explanation complexity adds 0.52 satisfaction for complex scenarios vs 0.24 for simple ones; interaction chi2(1)=11.52, p<.01; simple scenarios rated higher overall, chi2(1)=18.35). Study 4 n=253 (inconsistent details need more complex explanations, M 5.80 vs 5.23, chi2(1)=29.05).
limits: Online vignettes, self-report. Not a replication of a specific Lombrozo experiment; it changes the question.
agent_relevance: A simplicity weight should depend on how complex the observed data are. A fixed simplicity bonus for every problem is not supported.

source: Zemla, Sloman, Bechlivanidis, Lagnado (2017) Evaluating everyday explanations (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review)
finding: A different lab found that simplicity did not predict how good real-world explanations were rated. People preferred explanations that invoke more causal mechanisms.
numbers: Corpus from Reddit's Explain Like I'm Five and other sources; judged quality predicted from several criteria. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Correlational, real text, not a controlled manipulation.
agent_relevance: A limit on the human simplicity prior: in naturalistic explanation, completeness beat parsimony.

source: Johnson, Valenti, Keil (2019) Simplicity and complexity preferences in causal explanation: an opponent heuristic account (Cognitive Psychology)
finding: A second independent lab (Keil, Yale) finds people use simplicity as a cue to prior probability and complexity as a cue to goodness of fit, and that the simplicity preference shifts with context.
numbers: Five studies. Studies 2 and 3: stronger simplicity preference in deterministic than stochastic contexts. Studies 4 and 5: stronger for physical than social causal systems. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC).
agent_relevance: The human simplicity preference is real but moderated by causal texture; it is not a general-purpose prior to copy into an LLM pipeline.

source: Pacer and Lombrozo (2017) Ockham's razor cuts to the root: simplicity in causal explanation (JEP: General)
finding: Within the Lombrozo lab: preferences track root simplicity (how many unexplained causes) rather than node simplicity (how many causes). The preference is tempered, not removed, by probability favouring the complex option.
numbers: Four experiments. Committing to a less likely but simpler explanation distorted memory for past observations. Preference was larger when the root cause was strongly linked to its effects. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Same lab as the original 2007 result, so not independent.
agent_relevance: If an S7 simplicity term is used, count unexplained root assumptions, not the total number of causes.

source: Williams, Lombrozo, Rehder (2013) The hazards of explanation: overgeneralization in the face of exceptions (JEP: General)
finding: Explaining helps learning of broad patterns and hurts when the pattern has exceptions. Two category learning experiments across artifact and social domains.
numbers: Two experiments; sample sizes not read here. The LLM follow-up (Liu et al., d14) replicates the vehicle task.
limits: Abstract only. Lombrozo lab with an outside coauthor (Rehder).
agent_relevance: Human basis for gap 9. The LLM replication in d14 supports it for chain of thought.

source: Douven and Schupbach (2015) The role of explanatory considerations in updating (Cognition)
finding: Three experiments, as stated in the abstract, support the view that judged explanatory goodness enters people's belief updating beyond Bayes. A reanalysis of the older Schupbach urn study (N=26) is in the existing file (a14).
numbers: Numbers not read. The abstract says the results 'strongly support the predictive superiority of the explanationist position'.
limits: Abstract only. The authors defend the explanationist view; no outside-lab replication or failed replication was located in this search.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no independent replication or refutation of the updating result was found.

source: Wojtowicz and DeDeo (2020) From probability to consilience: how explanatory values implement Bayesian reasoning (Trends in Cognitive Sciences)
finding: Proposes that explanatory values (simplicity, scope, coherence and others) arise from one Bayesian framework, and that explanatory vices such as conspiracy theories follow from the same framework.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Abstract only. Theory paper.
agent_relevance: A principled reading of virtues as terms in a posterior: a link between the virtue scores and the prior and likelihood used in S7.

source: Steiglechner, Mahler, Lohmann (2026) LLMs Can See the Smoke but not the Fire (Elenchos) - results re-opened
finding: Models notice that a system was changed far more often than they name the cause. More reasoning effort helps only a little, and attribution drops sharply when changes interact.
numbers: Detection accuracy (VK) vs attribution accuracy (VA), mean over probes: GPT-5.4 VK 0.86, VA 0.37; GPT-5.4 low reasoning VA 0.41; medium VA 0.47 (VK 0.92); Gemini 2.5 Pro VK 0.93, VA 0.35; Claude Haiku 4.5 VK 0.78, VA 0.34; Mistral Large VK 0.65, VA 0.31. Accuracy falls with each step of less prompt information and with mutation count k.
limits: The authors flag the reasoning-budget finding as needing validation. Only low and medium effort were reported for GPT-5.4 in what was read.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models do not flatten the interacting-causes curve by themselves. A code-built diff of observed behaviour (S2) and an impasse step (S6) remain untested; this benchmark would be a good place to test them.

source: Maasch et al. (2025) Compositional Causal Reasoning Evaluation in Language Models
finding: Errors in propagating causal quantities through a graph grow with the number of mediating steps for all models tested except o1 (GPT-4o with CoT also did not rise monotonically but had very large error at six mediators).
numbers: For all models except GPT-4o with CoT and o1, mean relative absolute error rose monotonically with shortest path distance and number of mediators. GPT-4o with CoT had more than 10x the error for six mediators than for three. Only o1 was fully consistent across compositions. Models: Llama, Phi, GPT families.
limits: Forward causal arithmetic (average treatment effect, probability of necessity and sufficiency) in word problems, not abduction. Single task.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model can stay flat on composed causal steps, so the sharp fall for interacting causes in Elenchos is not inevitable. Different task from abduction, so weak evidence for gap 6.

source: Elmoznino, Marty, Kasetty, Gagnon, Mittal, Fathi, Sridhar, Lajoie (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor (ICML)
finding: In-context learning's next-token loss equals prequential code length, so minimising it trades fit against complexity. A built-in simplicity pressure exists in sequence models, in theory.
numbers: Theory plus small controlled experiments (for example Mastermind with GPT-4o at temperature 0). Task generalisation was harder in open-ended cases, where even a large pretrained LLM failed to learn in context a task a small MLP learns.
limits: Mostly theory and toy tasks. Does not test whether LLMs choose simpler explanations from a hypothesis pool.
agent_relevance: A weak argument that LLMs already lean simple. It does not say whether that is right for a given problem; the exceptions result (d14) says it can be wrong.

source: He, Wu, Zhang, Wan, Zhao, Du, Chen (2025) GEAR: a general evaluation framework for abductive reasoning - search for inference-time use
finding: The set-level scores (consistency, generalisation, diversity) were used to evaluate and to build a training signal with a momentum curriculum. No best-of-N or reranking at inference time was found in the text.
numbers: Keyword search of the full PDF for best-of, rerank, select, test-time and majority returned only training and curriculum content. Earlier files record that 70B-class models produce only 20% of fully consistent hypothesis sets and about 80% of equally plausible hypotheses are labelled incorrect.
limits: A keyword search, not a line-by-line read of every section. Absence of an experiment is not proof.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 is still untested. CodeT (d11) is the nearest proof that agreement-based selection scores work at inference time.
